questions.question: What pattern does each frontend question family test — and how do you structure each answer?
questions.title: Interview Pattern Map
questions.direct_answer: The question families with their evaluation targets: WHAT-IS (definition: one-sentence definition + mechanism + a concrete example + the boundary/limits — the 'explain X' answer skeleton); HOW-DOES-X-WORK (mechanism: the pipeline/flow from input to output, stepwise, with the diagram drawn unprompted); X-vs-Y (comparison: SAME basis of comparison across both — correctness, performance, DX, ecosystem — and a RECOMMENDATION with a condition, never neutral lists); BUILD-X (implementation: clarify requirements FIRST, state the data shape, edge cases + states (loading/error/empty) — the components that separate a working demo from production thinking); DEBUG-X (diagnosis: reproduce → isolate → observe → fix → prove — the systematic sequence beats guessing); BROWSER/PERF questions (the cost model: what work the browser does — network, script, layout, paint — and which tool measures it). The universal structure: ANSWER FIRST (the one-liner), then the mechanism, then the example, then the trade-off/limit — interviewers grade the first sentence most.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The map with answer skeletons:

```text
FAMILY               EVALUATES            SKELETON
'What is X?'        concept clarity      1-sentence definition →
                                          mechanism (how it works) →
                                          concrete example →
                                          boundary (when NOT to use)

'How does X work?'  mental model         the pipeline, stepwise, INPUT →
                                          TRANSFORM → OUTPUT (draw it:
                                          the unprompted diagram is a
                                          senior signal)

'X vs Y?'           judgment             SAME axes for both (correctness,
                                          perf, DX, ecosystem) →
                                          recommendation + CONDITION
                                          ('X when <case>; Y otherwise')
                                          — a neutral list answers nothing

'Build X'           engineering          requirements + assumptions FIRST
                                          (out loud) → data shape →
                                          component split →
                                          UI STATES: loading / error / empty /
                                          success (naming them unprompted:
                                          the production-readiness signal)

'Debug X'           methodology           reproduce → isolate → observe →
                                          fix → prove (a sequence beats
                                          a guess every time)

perf/browser        cost model            where the work happens (network /
                                          script / layout / paint) +
                                          the tool that measures it
```

The universal openers (the 3 most valuable seconds): lead with the ONE-SENTENCE answer, then expand ('Context is a value channel: a provider publishes, consumers read the nearest one above — here's the mechanism...'). Interviewers grade the first sentence for signal density: a crisp definition proves you can prioritize; a rambling warm-up buries it. If you need a second to think: restate the question precisely ('So — closures in loops and why they read stale values...') — bought time WITH structure, not filler.

The meta-skills that decide rounds: CLARIFY before building (requirements, constraints, scale — the #1 differentiator in practical rounds: candidates who code immediately vs candidates who ask 'what should happen when the list is empty?'); THINK OUT LOUD at decision points (the fork, not the syntax — 'I could fetch per keystroke or debounce; with a typeahead I debounce because...'); and CLOSE with trade-offs unprompted ('this design optimizes for X at the cost of Y — I'd revisit it if <condition>'). Those three habits score higher than a flawless implementation without them.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    F{question family} -->|what is| D[definition + mechanism + example + boundary]
    F -->|how works| M[pipeline input → transform → output; draw it]
    F -->|vs| C[same axes both + recommendation with condition]
    F -->|build| B[clarify first; states: loading error empty; data shape]
    F -->|debug| G[reproduce isolate observe fix prove]
    F -->|perf| P[cost model: which phase + which tool]
    OPEN[open with the one-liner] --> GRADE[first sentence carries the signal]
    CLARIFY[clarify before coding] --> DIFF[the top differentiator]
    TRADE[close with trade-offs unprompted] --> SENIOR[the senior marker]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The evaluation model (what interviewers actually write down): most rubrics score along axes — DEPTH (mechanism vs slogan: 'closures capture variables' vs the binding-vs-value distinction), STRUCTURE (did the answer have a shape — definition/flow/comparison — or was it an unsorted retrieval dump), COMMUNICATION (leading with the answer, thinking aloud at forks, closing with trade-offs), and PRODUCTION-SENSE (edge cases, states, error handling named unprompted). Knowing the axes is why the SAME knowledge lands differently across candidates — structure converts knowledge into evidence.

The follow-up cascade (where rounds are actually won or lost): every strong answer invites a probe — you say 're-render', they ask 'when exactly does React re-render a component?'; you say 'memoize', they ask 'what invalidates a useMemo?'. The prep strategy that generalizes: for each core concept, pre-author the NEXT question (the probe you'd ask if YOU were the interviewer) — one level deeper than your planned answer. That single habit converts shallow-but-fluent topics into defensible ones and reveals exactly where your depth stops.

The practical-round realities (the build-a-thing layer): time-boxed live coding rewards the SKELETON-FIRST approach (types/interfaces → data shape → the happy path rendering → states → interactions — you always have something working when time runs out, and the interviewer sees architecture before implementation); system-design-lite frontend rounds (design a search-as-you-type, an infinite feed, a modal system) score on: the data flow (who owns state, where it's cached, who re-renders), the failure surface (network races, cancellation, offline), and the a11y/i18n/perf NFRs NAMED without prompting — the same three layers as the theory questions, applied to a design. The through-line of every family: state the shape, state the flow, state the failure mode — then the code is a formality.
